items.stem: What does the data-minimisation principle require?

options.text: Collecting only the personal data necessary for the stated purpose
options.rationale: Correct: minimisation limits data to what the purpose needs.

options.text: Collecting as much data as possible for future use
options.rationale: That is the opposite of minimisation.
Retention should be limited, not indefinite.
Minimisation limits, it does not prohibit, collection.

items.explanation: Correct: minimisation means collecting only what the purpose requires.

items.stem: Which TWO are rights data subjects commonly have under GDPR? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The right of access to their personal data
options.rationale: Correct: individuals can request access to their data.

options.text: The right to erasure in certain circumstances
options.rationale: Correct: erasure applies under defined conditions.

options.text: The right to demand a company never keep any records
options.rationale: Organisations may need to retain certain records lawfully.

options.text: The right to set national law
options.rationale: Individuals do not legislate through data requests.

items.explanation: Correct: access and erasure (in defined circumstances) are recognised rights.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Is consent always the required lawful basis for processing personal data?

options.text: No; several lawful bases exist and consent is only one of them
options.rationale: Correct: contract, legal obligation and legitimate interests are among the alternatives.
Other lawful bases can apply depending on the purpose.

options.text: No; a lawful basis is never needed
options.rationale: A lawful basis is required for processing.

options.text: Yes; but only for public bodies
options.rationale: The range of lawful bases is not limited this way.

items.explanation: Correct: consent is one of several lawful bases, not always required.
